---
title: "Driving a preview"
description: >-
  Getting to the file, then driving three different previews: QLPreviewPanel on macOS, GNOME Sushi over D-Bus, QuickLook's named pipe on Windows, and the EPUB conversion.
---

Three systems, three mechanisms, one behaviour: press the key, the preview
appears; press it again, the preview goes away.

## Getting to the file

Before any of that, the attachment has to become a path — and under
*download as needed* it may not be a file on this machine at all. That setting
is the default for group libraries and a common choice for personal ones, and
under it most of a library is a database row until something asks for the file.
A preview is such an asking.

Zotero offers two accessors, and the difference between them is easy to read
the wrong way round. `getFilePath()` assembles the path the attachment should
have. `getFilePathAsync()` assembles it *and* checks the file is on disk,
answering `false` when it is not.

Reaching for the checking one first looks like the careful choice. It is the
trap: "there is no such attachment" and "the file has not been fetched yet"
come back as the same `false`, and the fetch that ought to follow sits behind a
branch nothing can reach. Nothing was previewable that had not already been
opened in Zotero once — silently, because a preview that never starts says
nothing. Zotero's own `viewAttachment` takes the synchronous accessor, and this
plugin now does the same:

1. `getFilePath()` for the path it should have.
2. `IOUtils.exists` here, where the answer can be acted on.
3. `Zotero.Sync.Runner.downloadFile` when the file is absent, the attachment is
   a stored one, and the library syncs files at all. A linked file that has
   gone missing has no copy on a server to fetch.
4. `getFilePathAsync()` afterwards — now that the file should be there, the
   checking accessor is the one that answers both whether it arrived and where
   it went.

A book or a scan is megabytes over the network, so the fetch shows a progress
window. Without one the plugin would look like it had ignored the keystroke,
which is exactly what a missing file looked like for as long as the fetch was
unreachable.

## macOS — QLPreviewPanel

The plugin launches a small bundled helper, `qlpreview`, which drives
`QLPreviewPanel` — the very panel the Finder shows. The subprocess handle is
retained, so pressing Space again, or Escape, closes the preview.

### Why not qlmanage

`/usr/bin/qlmanage -p` looks like the obvious answer and is not. It is a
debugging tool rather than the Finder's Quick Look, and it cannot show
everything the Finder can. On a video it dies outright:

```
NSInternalInconsistencyException
'Setting highlightedTimeRanges is not supported in your app.'
AVKitCore  -[AVPlayerItem setHighlightedTimeRanges:]
Movie      (/System/Library/QuickLook/Movie.qlgenerator)
```

Apple's own movie generator calls an AVKit method that AVKit refuses inside
`qlmanage`. Driving `QLPreviewPanel` instead renders whatever the Finder
renders, third-party Quick Look extensions included. `qlmanage` is kept only as
a fallback for the case where the helper cannot be deployed.

## Linux — GNOME Sushi over D-Bus

```sh
dbus-send --session --print-reply --reply-timeout=10000 \
  --dest=org.gnome.NautilusPreviewer \
  /org/gnome/NautilusPreviewer org.gnome.NautilusPreviewer.ShowFile \
  string:file:///path int32:0 boolean:true
```

::: {.callout-warning title="--print-reply is not there for its output"}
Leaving it off is not a small difference. Without it `dbus-send` writes the
message and exits within milliseconds. Sushi is started by D-Bus on demand and
takes about a second to come up, and `dbus-daemon` **discards a message queued
for an activation as soon as the connection that sent it goes away**. The
service then starts, is never told what to show, and quits again on its
twelve-second idle timeout.

Nothing appears and nothing is logged. The failure is completely silent, which
is what makes it worth a warning box. Waiting for the reply keeps the connection
open until the call has been delivered.
:::

The reply is also the only sign the plugin gets that the preview service
answered at all, so the exit status is checked and a refusal — Sushi not
installed, most likely — is named in the log rather than swallowed.

The call returns as soon as the window has been handed its file, rather than
staying alive for as long as the preview, so there is no process to hold and
kill. `ShowFile`'s last argument closes the preview when the same file is
already showing, which gives Space the same toggle it has on macOS. Sushi shows
one file at a time.

## Windows — QuickLook's named pipe

[QuickLook](https://github.com/QL-Win/QuickLook) listens on a named pipe,
`QuickLook.App.Pipe.<user SID>`. One UTF-8 line through it —

```
QuickLook.App.PipeMessages.Toggle|C:\path\file.pdf|
```

— shows the preview, the same line again dismisses it, and a different path
switches to that file. So Space has its toggle here too, again with no process
to hold.

The line is written straight from the plugin through **js-ctypes**: a handful of
Win32 calls, no helper binary, no subprocess, with the SID read from the process
token. Should Gecko ever drop ctypes, a PowerShell one-liner does the same
write; it reaches the shell as `-EncodedCommand`, so no execution policy and no
command-line quoting apply to it.

An earlier attempt at this integration
([QuickLook #584](https://github.com/QL-Win/QuickLook/issues/584), 2019)
foundered on exactly that SID, and its era's conclusion — that the Store build
is sandboxed away from the pipe — was repeated for years. Measured today,
neither holds: the Store package declares `runFullTrust` and answers the pipe
like the desktop build.

::: {.callout-caution title="Never probe the pipe"}
QuickLook's pipe reader takes a line per connection and dereferences whatever it
got. A client that connects and sends nothing — a `Test-Path` on the pipe path,
any is-it-there probe — **kills the listener**, silently, until QuickLook is
restarted.

The plugin therefore never probes. Every connection it makes carries one
complete line, and "QuickLook is not running" is learned from the connect
failing, which is when it is named in the log.
:::

## EPUB, everywhere

No system preview renders an EPUB, so this is the one format the plugin
transforms rather than hands over. Everything else — MOBI, DJVU, whatever a
preview extension claims — goes to the panel untouched.

The book is read **out of its archive**, through two readers the platform
already provides. Gecko's `nsIZipReader` opens the container; Zotero's own
`EPUB.mjs` — the module it uses for full-text indexing — joins the manifest to
the spine and yields the sections in reading order, already parsed. Each
chapter's `<body>` is appended into a single output document.

::: {.callout-note title="Why so little of this is ours"}
Until 1.2.0 the plugin spawned `/usr/bin/unzip`, or `tar.exe` on Windows, and
spread the book across a temp directory — a subprocess and its timeout for
something the platform does in-process, plus a directory to clean up. What
Zotero already maintains is now used instead. What it does **not** offer is a
converter: its EPUB reader is epub.js, which renders live in a Zotero window,
and a preview panel runs no scripts at all. So the assembly stays ours.
:::

The book's own stylesheets, linked and inline, are carried in as text so the
original layout survives, with a Palatino base font, an 80 px margin and a
720 px book-width column applied on top. Images, fonts and inline SVGs — named
in markup **and in CSS** — are written out into an `asset/` directory beside
the page, once each however often the book names them, and referred to
relatively from there.

::: {.callout-note title="Why not embedded in the page"}
They were, briefly, as `data:` URLs. That made the page self-contained, but
base64 costs a third more than the file it encodes and the whole book has to be
held as one string while it is built — which called for a size limit, and a
limit means a preview that shows part of a book. A preview of part of a book is
not a preview of that book. Written out beside the page there is nothing to
limit: the volume can be any size, and the store removes the entry whole when
its time comes.
:::

Parsing and assembly go through `DOMParser` and run on the document tree, so
scripts and inline event handlers are removed as **nodes** rather than matched
as text. A converted book is kept and reused until its file changes — see
[the store](contact-sheet.qmd).

### Annotations

Zotero keeps annotations in its database rather than in the file, for an EPUB
as for a PDF. The PDF path asks Zotero to bake them in — `PDFWorker.export`
writes a copy with the marks drawn on the page, and that copy is what the panel
shows. **There is no such export for an EPUB.** Zotero's reader draws them live
from an [EPUB CFI](https://idpf.org/epub/linking/cfi/), and the engine that
resolves a CFI lives inside the reader's own bundle, reachable only from the
reader.

So the CFI is read here, and written for one thing only — the link each tile
of a page overview carries back into the reader. `cfi.js` parses
it and resolves it against the spine document, which is exactly the tree the
CFI was written against and exactly what `getSectionDocuments()` hands over.
That is why the marking happens per section, **before** the page is assembled:
afterwards the tree the identifier describes no longer exists.

The package path names the spine item — `/6` the `<spine>` among the package's
children, `/14` the seventh `<itemref>` — and Zotero's own `annotationSortIndex`
begins with that same number, two independent statements of one fact. The rest
of the path walks the document to a text node, and the offsets are the extent.
They are drawn as Zotero draws them, not as it seemed reasonable to draw
them. Its reader styles an annotation in flowing text as

``` js
type === "underline" ? { textDecorationColor: color }
                     : { backgroundColor: color + "80" }
```

— so a highlight carries its colour at **half opacity**, the same alpha the
PDF canvas fills a highlight with, and an underline is a real underline in the
annotation's colour, 2 px thick at 2 px offset from the reader's own
stylesheet. A solid fill was what this did before: a purple or blue passage
became hard to read, and it looked unlike the document it came from. A range
crossing element boundaries becomes one wrapper per text node, which is what a
browser does with a selection.

The colour itself is whatever the annotation carries. Zotero offers eight, but
the field holds a string and plugins put their own palettes in it — a library
checked here had 232 of 500 annotations in colours Zotero never offers, from
[zotQDA](https://github.com/fre-ms/zotQDA). All of them are six-digit hex,
which is what Zotero's own reader requires too, since it appends the alpha as
two more digits exactly as this does. A three-digit form is written out first,
or the alpha would land inside the colour; anything else is passed on untouched
and without an alpha, because an unexpected notation should cost the right
opacity at worst, never the right colour.

::: {.callout-note title="epub.js, not the paper"}
A strict reading of EPUB CFI 1.1 interleaves elements and character data in one
numbering, so that odd steps address the text *between* elements. epub.js
counts text children among text children — and epub.js is what wrote every CFI
this will ever read. Matching the writer is what makes the answer right.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Nothing is dropped"}
A note carries no text to place, a comment belongs to no particular word, and a
highlight whose wording the markup broke differently cannot be found. All of
them appear in a list behind a button in the corner, in reading order, with
their colour and comment — and one that could not be placed is shown as such,
rather than quietly missing.

The quotation in an entry is marked as the passage is marked, which is what
Zotero does in its own annotation list: the same span with the same style,
`annotation-text` beside a menu button and a hint. A swatch alone says which
colour was used; this says what was done with it.

The menu opens **closed**, and each entry folds: the quotation is cut to two
lines by the stylesheet — measured in Quick Look, which renders the clamp — and
opening one shows the whole of it, the comment, and a link to the passage. One
copy of the text either way, cut where it is shown rather than where it is
built, so nothing is lost and nothing duplicated. A flex row puts the swatch
beside the first line, which takes the native disclosure marker away, so one is
drawn instead — steadier in any case across three engines that each draw their
own differently.

An entry whose passage **is** in the page links into it: the first piece of the
marked range carries an anchor, and the entry points at it. First in
reading order, not first wrapped — wrapping runs backwards, because splitting a
text node moves every offset after it, and a reader following the link should
arrive at the beginning of the passage rather than its end.
:::

### The table of contents

What is read is the navigation the book itself carries — **EPUB 3** keeps it in
a navigation document (the manifest item with `properties="nav"`), **EPUB 2** in
the NCX file the spine names in its `toc` attribute. Both are read, the newer
first. Titles and nesting are therefore the publisher's; ones derived from
headings would be guesses.

::: {.callout-note title="Why <details> and no script"}
macOS renders previews with **JavaScript disabled** and refuses ordinary
navigation, which appears to rule out a contents box that folds. It does not:
`<details>`/`<summary>` opens natively, without a line of script, and anchors
within the same page are followed.

Both were measured by clicking them in a real preview — the fold works, the jump
works. That is why the contents are built this way and not another.

The same element carries the **floating menu**: the `<summary>` is fixed to a
corner as a button, and opening it lays the list over the text instead of
pushing the book down. No script is involved in that either — `<details>` holds
the state itself, which is the only reason such a menu can exist in a panel
that runs none. Below 420 px the menus go back into the flow, where they cover
nothing.
:::

Each chapter is given an **anchor of its own** during assembly (`zotlook-ch0`,
`zotlook-ch1`, …). It is needed because the navigation often points at the file
alone and the book's own ids may be missing. Where an entry does point inside a
chapter, that is where it jumps — but only if the id really survives into the
assembled document; sanitising removes scripts and event attributes and leaves
ids alone.

A book with no usable navigation gets **no** box. The preview of a document
without chapters should look like the document, not like a feature that failed.

Because the plugin cannot reliably tell whether an EPUB preview extension is
installed, the conversion is a setting rather than a guess.
